Wet-bulb temperature — what a thermometer reads when wrapped in a wet cloth — folds humidity
into the reading, and it is the number that actually governs whether the human body can shed
heat. Past a critical wet-bulb value, sweat stops evaporating fast enough and core temperature
climbs without limit. This project maps how close 56 U.S. cities have come to that limit.

Building on my work with Georgia Tech's Urban Climate Lab on the
[Human Heat Tolerance Index](../urbanheat/), I pulled two decades of hourly NOAA NCEI Local
Climatological Data — 2005 through 2025, one primary airport station per city — and extracted
each city's hottest wet-bulb hour of every year, along with the dry-bulb temperature, relative
humidity and dew point that accompanied it. The result is an interactive D3 map: hover a city
for its record peak, its warming trend and a projection toward its critical threshold; click for
year-by-year detail with fitted trends.

### What it shows

The threshold follows the 2022 Penn State study (Vecellio et al., *Journal of Applied
Physiology*), which tested the long-assumed 35 °C limit and found the real ceiling for healthy
young adults is closer to **31 °C (~87 °F)** in humid conditions — and lower still, about
**28 °C (~82 °F)**, in dry heat, where danger arrives through extreme dry-bulb temperature at
low humidity. The map applies both, sorting cities into humid and arid regimes.

Two arguments run through the piece. The first is about what the number would actually *mean*:
87 °F wet-bulb is not the point at which heat becomes unpleasant, it is the point at which a
healthy adult doing almost nothing can no longer hold core temperature steady — so outdoor
construction, trash collection, school sports, delivery work and emergency response all become
unsafe well before it. The second is about how to read a trend line. The fitted slopes are noisy
and mostly point past 2100, which invites the wrong conclusion. But these are annual *maxima* —
spikes, not plateaus — and a threshold is crossed by a single hour, not an average year. Yearly
peaks scatter about 1.4 °F around their own trend lines, every one of the 56 cities has recorded
a peak above its current trend value, 23 are already within 3 °F of their threshold, and Phoenix
has touched its 82 °F arid line. As the line rises beneath a scatter that stays just as wide,
the odds of one dangerous hour climb far faster than any "projected year" suggests.

### Method notes

- **Data:** NOAA NCEI LCD hourly `FM-15` observations, 2005–2025, cleaned and concatenated per city.
- **Trends:** OLS slope of annual maxima against year, reported per decade with R². These fits are
  deliberately presented as illustrations of a current slope rather than forecasts — the R² values
  are low because year-to-year variation dwarfs the long-term signal.
- **Built with:** R for the data pipeline, D3 and TopoJSON for the map. The site is a single
  self-contained HTML file with the city data and U.S. geometry inlined.
